title: אונקלוס הגר

paragraphs: Onkelos the convert, Titus’s sister’s son, a tanna of a baraita, chapter Hamokher Peirot 99a: “Cherubs, a work of play.” He received from Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua (Megillah, chapter 1) and translated the Torah from their mouths. Shalshelet Hakkabbalah 28 likewise writes this, and found written that it was year 3868. Rashi, Kiddushin, chapter 2, 49a: Onkelos’s additions were not his own invention, since it was given at Sinai; rather, it was improved, and he re-established it [the cited Rashi reads “it was forgotten”] (see Semag, positive commandments, section 19). Tzemach David, at חייא ב״א תת״מ [locator/date text unclear], and Me'or Einayim, chapter 45, write that the Onkelos who translated the Torah is not Titus’s nephew: this one converted in Hillel and Shammai’s days and lived long. See Zohar, Acharei Mot, at עקל״א [locator unresolved]: Hillel and Shammai told Onkelos they would not teach him Torah before he was circumcised. He saw Yonatan ben Uzziel, who translated the Prophets (see there and Aquilas the convert). Responsa Halakhot Ketannot, part 2, section 170, writes: the Torah’s and Prophets’ Targum is a law given to Moses at Sinai; the Writings’ Targum is not such a law, but Yonatan ben Uzziel said it. See Tosafot, Megillah 21b, s.v. Uvamegillah: Yonatan did not make it; it dates from the tannaim.

Yuchasin 159b writes that he was Rabbi Gamliel of Yavneh’s student; Abarbanel, introduction to Nachalat Avot, likewise. (I do not know whence he derives this.) Tosefta, Kelim: Onkelos the convert’s cook brought his bread before Rabban Gamliel. He burned Rabban Gamliel the elder’s bed and personal effects in his honor (see there). He entered before Rabbi Eliezer (Bereshit Rabbah, section 70; Bamidbar, end of section 8). Tosefta, Demai, chapter 8: being stringent with himself, he took to the Dead Sea what he inherited with his brother. Gilgulei Neshamot writes: Onkelos the convert was an ibbur, a soul-infusion, of Eliphaz son of Esau. Eliphaz would not kill Jacob at his father’s command, but took all his possessions. Likewise Onkelos sought Titus’s advice and did not heed it (see there). Thus perhaps casting his inheritance into the Dead Sea repaired taking all Jacob’s money.
